raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular myocardial deposition of misfolded amyloid fibrils. The two dominant forms are immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidosis (AL), driven by a clonal plasma-cell disorder, and transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), caused either by pathogenic TTR variants or age-related wild-type transthyretin misfolding [1,2]. Although once considered rare, cardiac amyloidosis is now recognized as an important and underdiagnosed cause of heart failure, arrhythmia, aortic stenosis, and multisystem disease in older adults [3-8].

Pathophysiologically, AL amyloidosis combines mechanical infiltration with direct light-chain cardiotoxicity, often producing rapidly progressive heart failure and high early mortality if untreated [1,16,17]. ATTR cardiomyopathy is typically more indolent, but progressive amyloid accumulation causes ventricular thickening, diastolic dysfunction, atrial myopathy, conduction disease, and ultimately systolic impairment [2,18,19]. Wild-type ATTR is particularly enriched among older men and may be preceded by “red flags” such as bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, atrial fibrillation, low-flow aortic stenosis, or unexplained heart failure with preserved ejection fraction [5-8].

Clinically, patients often present with exertional dyspnea, edema, fatigue, orthostatic symptoms, syncope, or disproportionate biomarker elevation. Electrocardiography may show low voltage, pseudo-infarction patterns, atrioventricular block, or atrial arrhythmias; however, voltage can be normal, especially in ATTR. Echocardiography commonly reveals increased wall thickness, biatrial enlargement, restrictive filling, thickened valves, pericardial effusion, and reduced longitudinal strain with relative apical sparing, a useful diagnostic clue [15]. Cardiac magnetic resonance adds tissue characterization: diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement, abnormal gadolinium kinetics, high native T1, and increased extracellular volume support the diagnosis and provide prognostic information [12-14].

Modern diagnosis depends on rapidly distinguishing AL from ATTR, because AL is a hematologic emergency. All suspected cases require serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation. If monoclonal testing is negative and bone-avid tracer scintigraphy shows grade 2–3 myocardial uptake, ATTR cardiomyopathy can be diagnosed noninvasively without biopsy [9-11]. If monoclonal proteins are present, scintigraphy is not sufficiently specific; tissue confirmation with amyloid typing, preferably by mass spectrometry or validated immunohistochemistry, is required [9,30]. Genetic testing is mandatory after ATTR diagnosis to distinguish hereditary from wild-type disease and to guide family screening.

Prognosis varies by amyloid type and disease stage. In AL amyloidosis, cardiac troponin, natriuretic peptides, and involved–uninvolved free light-chain difference define staging systems that predict early death and guide treatment intensity [16,17]. In ATTR, natriuretic peptides, renal function, and functional status are central prognostic markers; validated staging systems separate patients into clinically meaningful risk groups [18,19]. Intracardiac thrombus may occur even in sinus rhythm, reflecting severe atrial mechanical dysfunction, so anticoagulation decisions often require a lower threshold than in nonamyloid cardiomyopathy [29].

Management combines supportive heart-failure care with amyloid-specific therapy. Diuretics remain the mainstay for congestion, while beta-blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, and calcium-channel blockers are often poorly tolerated because of fixed stroke volume, autonomic dysfunction, or conduction disease. Pacemakers are frequently required for conduction disease, though defibrillator benefit is less certain and should be individualized. Multidisciplinary care is essential.

In AL amyloidosis, treatment aims at rapid suppression of the plasma-cell clone. Melphalan-dexamethasone, proteasome inhibitor–based regimens, autologous stem-cell transplantation in selected patients, and, most recently, daratumumab-containing therapy have substantially improved hematologic and organ responses [20-23]. Early diagnosis remains critical because advanced cardiac AL may progress faster than therapy can reverse.

In ATTR cardiomyopathy, tafamidis, a transthyretin tetramer stabilizer, reduced mortality, cardiovascular hospitalization, and functional decline in symptomatic ATTR cardiomyopathy and is now foundational disease-modifying therapy [24]. Gene-silencing approaches, including patisiran and inotersen, reduce hepatic transthyretin production and improved neurologic outcomes in hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy; patisiran also showed favorable cardiac biomarker and imaging signals in patients with cardiac involvement [25-27]. In vivo CRISPR-Cas9 editing has demonstrated profound transthyretin reduction in early studies, suggesting a future of one-time gene-directed therapy [28].

Overall, cardiac amyloidosis has shifted from a postmortem curiosity to a treatable cardiomyopathy. The key clinical challenge is recognition: older patients with unexplained ventricular thickening, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial arrhythmia, aortic stenosis, carpal tunnel syndrome, or discordant electrocardiographic and echocardiographic findings should trigger structured evaluation. Timely typing of amyloid and initiation of targeted therapy can alter the natural history of both AL and ATTR disease.
